Here we provide the windows in which our (naive) implementation of sign (via logistic function approximation) has an error of $10\%$ or less. Error is calculated based off of a target of $0$ or $1$. The target is set to $0$ for an input $x \lt \frac{1}{2}$ and $1$ for input $x \gt \frac{1}{2}$. The error is the absolute difference between the target and approximate values expressed as a percentage.

|----:|:---------:|:----------:|:------------:|
|  1  | [-2.543, -2.210] | [2.210, 2.543] | 0.333 |
|  2  | [-1.272, -1.105] | [1.105, 1.272] | 0.167 |
|  4  | [-0.636, -0.553] | [0.553, 0.636] | 0.083 |
|  8  | [-0.318, -0.277] | [0.277, 0.318] | 0.041 |
| 16  | [-0.159, -0.139] | [0.139, 0.159] | 0.020 |
| 32  | [-0.079, -0.070] | [0.070, 0.079] | 0.009 |
| 64  | [-0.040, -0.035] | [0.035, 0.040] | 0.005 |

![sigmoid_accuracy_ring](https://hackmd.io/_uploads/rJfsCM9ZMg.png)


Now we present the analogous accuracy windows for hyperbolic tangent as previously described for the logistic function. Error is calculated in the same manner. 

It is worth noting that these accuracy windows are about half the size compared to those of the logistic function. This is due to the radii of convergence being $\pi/2$ and $\pi$ for hyperbolic tangent and logistic respectively. Hence, hyperbolic tangent is naturally steeper than logistic and approximates the real value faster on a similar interval.

:::info
**Remark**: we can see a higher $k$ compresses the interval of high accuracy towards 0. We note that given the right compression method for a dataset we could approximate a reasonable sign value for the whole dataset. Requiring a user input of known maximum and minimum value of the input (beyond $(-\infty,\infty)$ ) would support this scaling. [^prantl]
:::

Within our current experimentation we found the window of high accuracy convergence scaled in proportion to the window of convergence, roughly $15\%$ of the observed data. 

### Inequality and Equality

Inequality and sign functions are essentially equivalent. If we have an useful sign function, we can effectively do an "inequality" function as follows:
$$(x > a) := \mathtt{sign}_{0, 1, a} (x),$$ which returns $1$ for each element $x_i$ of the vector $x$ if $x_i > a$ or $0$ otherwise. Of course, problems may happen very close to $a$, so one must be careful while using it in the construction of other operations.

With this, we can do an "equality" function. Because we are doing floating point arithmetic, it is inadvisable to do a "true equality" check, so what we mean when we say "$x$ is equal to $a$" means that their difference is small (up to an error $\epsilon$). This can be done via
$$(x == a) := (x > a-\epsilon) * (x < a+\epsilon),$$ which gives $1$ exactly when both conditions are met; that is, $x$ is within $\epsilon$ of $a$ and $0$ otherwise. As an example, $$(x_i == 0) := (x_i\ge-0.01)*(x_i\le0.01)$$  obtains a $0$-$1$ vector, which has $1$ in place $i$ if and only if $x_i$ is close (within $0.01$) to $0$.
